The Change-of-Basis Matrix

After several years, I finally understand the change-of-basis matrix.

Published

17 September 2026

I recently came across a linear algebra problem about change of basis, which went something like this:

Problem: Let Bold={(10),(11)}B_{old} = \{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\}Bold​={(10​),(11​)} and Bnew={(−11),(01)}B_{new} = \{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\}Bnew​={(−11​),(01​)} be bases for R2\R^2R2. Find the change of basis matrix from BoldB_{old}Bold​ to BnewB_{new}Bnew​.

To be completely honest, I kinda forgot what the change-of-basis matrix was supposed to look like (I’m pretty rusty on my linear algebra). I didn’t want to just look it up though, so I tried to figure it out. My thought process went as follows:

Solution(?): Changing basis means that if I have some vector expressed in terms of BoldB_{old}Bold​, then I want to figure out how that same vector would be expressed in terms of BnewB_{new}Bnew​. What exactly does it mean to express a vector in terms of a basis? Well, every vector has a unique representation as a linear combination of basis vectors. Let’s first label the basis vectors of BoldB_{old}Bold​ as u1,u2u_1, u_2u1​,u2​ and label the basis vectors of BnewB_{new}Bnew​ as v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​. So in more precise terms, changing basis would mean that if we have a arbitrary vector www which is represented in terms of the old basis as (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​), i.e. w=au1+bu2w=au_1+bu_2w=au1​+bu2​, then I want to translate it into a linear combination of v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​ to get the representation of the same object in the new basis.

So how can I do that? Well, I thought that since www is a linear combination of u1,u2u_1,u_2u1​,u2​, then I should first figure out what u1,u2u_1,u_2u1​,u2​ are as linear combinations of v1,v2v_1,v_2v1​,v2​, since if u1=c1v1+c2v2u_1 = c_1v_1 + c_2v_2u1​=c1​v1​+c2​v2​ and
u2=d1v1+d2v2u_2 = d_1v_1+d_2v_2u2​=d1​v1​+d2​v2​, then

w=au1+bu2=a(c1v1+c2v2)+b(d1v1+d2v2)=(ac1+bd1)v1+(ac2+bd2)v2\begin{aligned} w &= au_1+bu_2 \\ &= a(c_1v_1+c_2v_2)+b(d_1v_1+d_2v_2) \\ &= (ac_1+bd_1)v_1+(ac_2+bd_2)v_2 \end{aligned}w​=au1​+bu2​=a(c1​v1​+c2​v2​)+b(d1​v1​+d2​v2​)=(ac1​+bd1​)v1​+(ac2​+bd2​)v2​​

In other words, www is represented as (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​) in the old basis, and in the new basis this becomes (ac1+bd1ac2+bc2)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}ac_1+bd_1\\ ac_2+bc_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ac1​+bd1​ac2​+bc2​​).

So now the task has turned into figuring out what the cic_ici​ and did_idi​ are supposed to be. Writing
u1=c1v1+c2v2u_1=c_1v_1+c_2v_2u1​=c1​v1​+c2​v2​ out in terms of the concrete vectors gives us

(10)=c1(−11)+c2(01)=(−c1c1+c2)=(−1011)(c1c2)\begin{aligned} \left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right) &= c_1\left(\begin{matrix}-1\\1\end{matrix}\right) + c_2\left(\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-c_1\\ c_1+c_2\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-1&0\\1&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{matrix}\right) \end{aligned}(10​)​=c1​(−11​)+c2​(01​)=(−c1​c1​+c2​​)=(−11​01​)(c1​c2​​)​

Now we can just solve for (c1c2)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)(c1​c2​​) using basic linear algebra techniques to find that c1=−1c_1=-1c1​=−1 and c2=1c_2=1c2​=1. A similar argument shows that d1=−1d_1=-1d1​=−1 and d2=2d_2=2d2​=2.

Putting everything together, we have that w=(−a−b)v1+(a+2b)v2w = (-a-b)v_1+(a+2b)v_2w=(−a−b)v1​+(a+2b)v2​, giving us the representation of www in terms of the new basis, i.e. (−a−ba+2b)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−a−ba+2b​).

With so many different ways to refer to www now, I’m going to formalize it by letting wold=(ab)w_{old}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wold​=(ab​) and wnew=(−a−ba+2b)w_{new} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wnew​=(−a−ba+2b​). www will be reserved for talking about the object itself, independent of any basis. If this sounds redundant, remember that woldw_{old}wold​ and wneww_{new}wnew​ are just descriptions of www. Think of it as www being an apple, and woldw_{old}wold​ and wneww_{new}wnew​ being the words “apple” in English and “蘋果” in Chinese. The two words both refer to the same object, the apple, but neither of them are actually the apple.

To recap, we started with an arbitrary vector www’s coordinate representation in terms of the old basis
(woldw_{old}wold​) and then did some calculations to obtain www’s coordinate representation in terms of the new basis (wneww_{new}wnew​). Now to get the change-of-basis matrix, we need to figure out how to get from woldw_{old}wold​ to wneww_{new}wnew​. This is quite easy, since we can simply use matrix multiplication to decompose wneww_{new}wnew​ as follows:

(−a−ba+2b)=(−1−112)(ab)\left(\begin{matrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)(−a−ba+2b​)=(−11​−12​)(ab​)

Let A=(−1−112)A = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(−11​−12​). Then we have that wnew=Awoldw_{new} = Aw_{old}wnew​=Awold​, so AAA must be the change-of-basis matrix. □\square□.

Well that wasn’t too hard, was it? Except it’s WRONG!!! I looked on Wikipedia afterwards and found that the actual change-of-basis matrix should be the inverse of AAA, which would be (−2−111)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-2&-1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−21​−11​). If we call this matrix BBB, then the relationship we obtain is wold=Bwneww_{old} = Bw_{new}wold​=Bwnew​.

But doesn’t that seem really weird? Like, now we have a vector expressed in terms of the new basis, and after applying the change-of-basis matrix, we get expression of that vector in the old basis. In other words, it seems like we’re transitioning from the new basis to the old basis, which should be the opposite of what we want. This really confused me, and I’m pretty sure it confused me when I learned about it initially too (which is probably why I couldn’t remember how it worked).

Things become clearer if we’re transitioning from the standard basis. These basis vectors we’ve been working with are themselves expressed in terms of the standard basis, which kind of obscures what’s going on. So let’s do the problem again, but instead we’ll transition from the standard basis, E={(10),(01)}E = \{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\}E={(10​),(01​)} to BoldB_{old}Bold​.

Solution: Let e1,e2e_1,e_2e1​,e2​ denote the standard basis vectors. We’ll do this exactly the same way, so we’ll first need to find out what the coordinate representations of e1,e2e_1,e_2e1​,e2​ are in terms of BoldB_{old}Bold​; i.e. figure out what c1,c2,d1,d2c_1,c_2,d_1,d_2c1​,c2​,d1​,d2​ are but for this particular case. This can be done pretty easily with some trial and error since the vectors are simple: c1=1,c2=0,d1=−1,d2=1c_1=1,c_2=0,d_1=-1,d_2=1c1​=1,c2​=0,d1​=−1,d2​=1 (in other words, with respect to BoldB_{old}Bold​, e1e_1e1​ is (10)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right)(10​) and e2e_2e2​ is (−11)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−11​)). Then for some vector www with standard coordinate representation (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​), we have

w=ae2+be2=au1+b(−u1+u2)=(a−b)u1+bu2\begin{aligned} w &= ae_2+be_2 \\ &= au_1+b(-u_1+u_2) \\ &= (a-b)u_1+bu_2 \end{aligned}w​=ae2​+be2​=au1​+b(−u1​+u2​)=(a−b)u1​+bu2​​

This means that wold=(a−bb)w_{old} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}a-b\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wold​=(a−bb​). Then

(a−bb)=(1−101)(ab)\left(\begin{matrix}a-b\\ b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)(a−bb​)=(10​−11​)(ab​)

Taking the inverse of this 2×22 \times 22×2 matrix, we get that A=(1101)A = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(10​11​) is our change-of-basis matrix. □\square□.

Well this is interesting, because this time this inverted matrix doesn’t seem weird to me at all. This matrix encodes the linear transformation which sends (10)\spmat{1\\0}(10​) to (10)\spmat{1\\0}(10​) and (01)\spmat{0\\1}(01​) to (11)\spmat{1\\1}(11​). In other words, AAA quite literally changes the basis EEE into BoldB_{old}Bold​.
